analysis.one_liner: Bans stock trading by members of Congress, the president, Supreme Court justices, and Fed officials.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to a Senate committee and never received a hearing, vote, or floor action before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would bar individual stock, commodity, and cryptocurrency trading by Members of Congress, the President and Vice President, Supreme Court justices, and top Federal Reserve officials, with violators facing a civil penalty of at least 10% of the trade's value. It would also require officials to disclose any loans, contracts, or grants they, their spouses, or their children receive from the federal government, and it would make financial disclosures searchable, sortable, and downloadable online. The existing STOCK Act has no automatic fine for late filings; this bill would add a $500 fine per missed report.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary citizens gain clearer visibility into whether their elected and appointed officials are using their positions to profit in financial markets, and more confidence that officials' personal finances do not overlap with federal money.

how_it_helps.text: Bars Members of Congress, the President, the Vice President, Supreme Court justices, Federal Reserve governors, and Fed bank presidents from individually trading stocks, commodities, futures, or cryptocurrency, with violators owing a civil penalty of at least 10% of the trade's value.

Requires covered officials to report applications for or receipt of federal loans, contracts, grants, and similar payments by them, their spouses, or dependent children within 30 days, with a $500 fine for failure to report.

Requires Members' and senior officials' financial disclosures to be posted online in searchable, sortable, downloadable formats accessible through an application programming interface, and extends electronic filing and disclosure requirements to federal judges and Federal Reserve bank officers.

Adds an automatic $500 fine each time an official fails to file a required transaction report under the STOCK Act, replacing the previous setup in which late filings generally carried no automatic penalty.

analysis.who_pays: Incumbent senior officials lose the ability to trade individual stocks and must divest within 180 days or place holdings in blind trusts; offices administering the system bear compliance costs.
analysis.who_pays_short: Members of Congress and senior officials

drawbacks.text: The enforcement fines are modest: $500 for a missed report and a penalty floor of 10% of a violated trade's value, which wealthy officials could absorb as a cost of doing business.
Officials may keep holdings acquired before taking office and can place securities in qualified blind trusts, so conflicts of interest may persist indirectly rather than disappear.

Supporters of a narrower approach argue a blanket ban on widely owned assets may discourage some experienced people from seeking office; the bill addresses this only by allowing blind trusts, not by alternatives such as longer mandatory holding periods.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — removing the ability of the people who write laws and set monetary policy to trade on information they help shape — is significant and directly tied to public trust in government. The main honest caveat is enforcement: the fines are small enough that a determined official could treat them as a fee, and blind trusts and pre-office holdings leave room for indirect conflicts. Still, the disclosure upgrades and the trading ban address a problem the public consistently ranks as important.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, which took no further action before the 117th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Kirsten Gillibrand introduced the bill in the Senate on February 9, 2022, with no cosponsors.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs.
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote followed, and the bill died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Senior officeholders keep the ability to trade individual stocks and the existing disclosure system, including the lack of automatic fines for late filings; no other group benefits measurably from the bill's failure.

for.name: Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand
for.role: U.S. Senator from New York, sole sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the Senate and gave it its only sponsorship.

against.name: Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; chaired by a Democrat in this Congress
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no further action — no hearing, markup, or committee vote — before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: With a single sponsor, zero cosponsors, and no votes or recorded opposition, the record shows no partisan pattern either way.

industries.industry: Members of Congress and other covered senior officials (President, Supreme Court justices, Federal Reserve leaders)
industries.note: The bill would strip these officeholders of the ability to trade individual stocks and would force public disclosure of federal payments to them and their families. Their interest in keeping those practices runs directly against the public's interest in transparent, conflict-free government. Not an industry in the commercial sense, but the concentrated interest the bill targets.

industries.industry: Federal financial disclosure and ethics offices
industries.note: The bill would assign these offices new duties — building searchable online databases, processing new filings, and issuing fines — while giving them clear authority to administer blind trusts and guidance. Their interest runs with the bill's transparency goals, at a real administrative cost.
